outcome: Perimeter policy is written in terms of applications rather than ports, with inline threat prevention reaching inspected traffic.
overview: Government perimeter rules written in terms of ports say what may pass but not what it is, and over years the base grows until nobody removes anything. PA-Series firewalls identify the application behind a session and apply policy to that, so a rule can permit a specific service rather than a port that several things happen to share. The migration is where the value is created or lost: converting port rules mechanically produces a modern platform running the old posture, which is why the share of rules genuinely rewritten is an acceptance criterion here.

benefits.text: Policy is expressed in terms of the application rather than the port it happens to use
benefits.limits: Only for applications the identification engine recognises; unrecognised or custom traffic remains port-based and should be listed rather than assumed covered

benefits.text: Threat prevention runs inline on identified sessions rather than on unclassified flows
benefits.limits: Inline prevention on encrypted traffic requires decryption, and the decryption policy is where most of the design effort actually goes

benefits.text: The same operating system covers appliance, virtual and container form factors as workloads move
benefits.limits: Policy portability is real; throughput is not, and each form factor must be sized on its own measured traffic

residency: Appliances, management and logs remain inside the entity’s own estate; no session content leaves the jurisdiction in this design

notFor.situation: An entity already running application-aware policy on another vendor’s platform
notFor.why: The capability is the same; replacing it means rewriting the rule base for no new function

notFor.situation: A boundary where decryption is prohibited and most traffic is encrypted
notFor.why: Application identification and inline prevention both degrade sharply without decryption

scope:
Model: Redington solutions engineering with an accredited Palo Alto Networks implementation partner · Duration: 8–12 weeks depending on rule-base size and window availability
Support model: Vendor hardware and subscription support with a replacement term appropriate to government criticality; Redington coordinates the vendor case.
1) Analyse — rule export, permissive-rule identification, traffic profiling with decryption impact measured
2) Rewrite — rules expressed as application policy, exclusions listed, decryption policy agreed
3) Rehearse — cutover runbook validated with a rollback path
4) Cut over and hand over — migration executed in window, central management established, operations handed over
deliverables: The measured share of rules expressed as application policy meets the figure agreed at design
The decryption policy names, per category, what is inspected and what is excluded and why
Logs record the identified application for permitted sessions, verified by sampling
effort: 8–12 weeks depending on rule-base size and window availability
